--- title: "Module 10: Survey Sampling" subtitle: "Terminology, Types of Samples, and Simple Random Sampling" format: revealjs: # theme: simple # other modern-ish options: dark, simple, solarized theme: simple slide-number: c/t # chalkboard: true # lets you draw on top of slides (keyboard: c) or open a board (b) width: 1200 height: 675 css: modern-slides.css auto-stretch: false html-math-method: mathjax execute: warning: false message: false echo: true include-in-header: --- ::: {.cell} ::: # Survey Sampling Terminology :::callout-note Lecture based on *Sampling Design and Analysis 3rd Edition* by Sharon L. Lohr Chapters 1, 2, and 15. Figures are from this text or recreated based on figures from the text unless otherwise noted! ::: ## Example: Literary Digest Poll (Activity 9.1) The Literary Digest boasted that they polled **10 million** voters across the 48 states in the US in October 1936. For each voter polled, they sent out a "straw ballot" and asked that it be mailed back once completed. Out of the **2.3 million ballots returned**, 1,293,699 said they planned to vote for for Landon, and 972,897 for Roosevelt. The list of 10 million voters primarily came from car registration lists and telephone books. (Source: [Squire, 1988](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2749114)) ![](../3-activities/_images/09.1-literary-digest.png){width=40%} ## Building Blocks - **Observational unit:** (or **element** or **measurement unit**): object on which a measurement is taken - **Target population:** complete collection of observations we want to study ($N$) - **Sample** subset of a population ($n$) ## Sampling Terminology - **Sampling unit:** The unit **actually sampled** - Non-overlapping collections fo elements from the population that cover the entire population. - When might observational units and sampling units be different?
- **Sampling frame:** A list of sampling units from which a sample may be selected. - Rare to have a sampling frame with every element of the population! ## Sampling Terminology - **Sampled population** the collection of all possible observational units that *might have* been chosen in a sample; the population from which the sample was *actually* taken. - **Sample** (refining this): collection of sampling units drawn from the sampling frame(s) ## Putting it All Together ![](_images/10.1-populations.png){width=90%} # Types of Sampling ## Probability Sampling - Each unit in the population has a known probability of selection - Relatedly, each possible **sample** from the population has a known probability of selection - The probabilities of all possible **samples** sum to 1. - Randomization mechanism used to choose units - Able to assess the variability (therefore precision) of statistics calculated from the sample - Avoid sampling bias ## Non-probability Sampling - Does not involve any form of random select - Representative?? - Examples: - Convenience sampling - Quota sampling - Judgement sampling ## Convenience sampling - Primary consideration for selecting the sample is how easy it is to recruit the units - Examples: :::columns :::{.column width=20%} ![](https://logos-world.net/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/Pepsi-Cola-Logo-1950-1962-700x394.png){fig-alt="pepsi logo on a bottle cap"} ::: :::{.column width=80%} ::: ::: ## Quota Sampling - Population is divided into different sub-populations and specified numbers (quotas) of units are required in each sub-population - Example: - Population: 23% first years, 23% 2nd, 23% 3rd, 23% 4th, 8% other years - Sample size: 200 - continue sampling until you get the required \% in each group and then you stop. ## Quota Sampling Example - Link, H. C., & Hopf, H. A. (1946). *People and books; a study of reading and book-buying habits.* Book Manufacturers Institute. - Quota factors: area, city size, age, sex, and socioeconomic status - Psychologist determined the blocks of the city - Interview people from a specified socioeconomic group. - Interviewers were allowed to choose the specific households. - n = 4,000 ## Quota Sampling Example - Found... 31% of “active readers” had bought the last book they read \& - ... 25% of all last books read cost $1 or less. - But ... ![Source: Sampling Design and Analysis 3rd Edition by Sharon L Lohr](_images/10.1-reading-table.png){width=60%} ... oversampled more educated readers ## Judgement Sampling - The people conducting the survey use "judgement'' to decide which population units are included in the sample
- Example: [Rivera (2016)](https://rucore.libraries.rutgers.edu/rutgers-lib/49079/) - investigating residents' experiences with applying for and obtaining federal disaster aid ## Judgement Sampling -- Example Hurricane Sandy :::columns :::{.column width=80%} - judgement sample of six New Jersey municipalities >These cities were chosen because they are located on the coast, and they all experienced similar disaster affects, such as damages due to flooding, storm surge, and windshear. [Rivera (2016)](https://rucore.libraries.rutgers.edu/rutgers-lib/49079/) - then random digit dialing used to get a random sample *within* each ::: :::{.column width=20%} ![Cities included in Rivera 2016 Focus Group Sampling](_images/101-nj-study.png) ::: ::: ## Probability Sampling Examples - simple random sampling - systematic sampling - stratified sampling - cluster sampling - ... # Simple Random Sampling ## Reminder: Probability Sampling - Each element in the population has a known probability of selection - To be representative, this probability needs to be greater than 0 - So... each possible **sample** from the population has a known probability of selection - The probabilities of each sample being drawn add to 1 (one) ## Framework for Probability Sampling - Consider the finite population of $N = 4$ units: $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ - Possible samples of $n=2$?
- There are $\binom{N}{n} = \frac{N!}{n!(N-n)!}$ possible samples of size $n$ that can be drawn with out replacement from a population of size $N$ ## Framework for Probability Sampling - Each possible sample $\mathcal{S}$ has a known probability of being chosen $P(\mathcal{S})$ - The differences in how we assign these probabilities is what distinguishes different probability sampling designs! Example samples: $\mathcal{S}_1 = \{1,2\}, \mathcal{S}_2 = \{1,3\}, \mathcal{S}_3 = \{1,4\}, \mathcal{S}_4 = \{2,3\}, \mathcal{S}_5 = \{2,4\}, \mathcal{S}_6 = \{3,4\}$ ## Inclusion Probability - What is the probability of each individual unit being sampled? $$\pi_i = P(\text{unit } i \text{ in the sample})$$ - $\pi_i$: sum the probabilities of all possible samples that include unit $i$ Example samples: $\mathcal{S}_1 = \{1,2\}, \mathcal{S}_2 = \{1,3\}, \mathcal{S}_3 = \{1,4\}, \mathcal{S}_4 = \{2,3\}, \mathcal{S}_5 = \{2,4\}, \mathcal{S}_6 = \{3,4\}$ ## Simple Random Sample Without Replacement (SRS) - Simplest (pun not(?) intended) probability sample - **SRS:** Every possible subset of $n$ units from the population of $N$ units has an **equal probability** of being sampled. $$P(\mathcal{S}) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{n}}$$ $\pi_i = \frac{\text{total number of samples that contain unit } i}{\text{total number of samples of size } n}$ ## Simple Random Sample in R :::columns :::column With a dataset: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nrow(airquality) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 153 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sample_air <- airquality |> slice_sample(n = 20, replace = F) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sample_air ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: ::: :::column With a vector: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ids_vec <- 1:100 sample_ids <- sample(ids_vec, size = 20, replace = F) sample_ids ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 4 33 30 60 44 75 81 51 97 32 82 14 24 41 98 5 83 3 46 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: # Goals of Survey Sampling and Types of Errors ## Why are we doing all of this!? - Want to learn about the world! - **Estimate** something about our **population** - We want to these estimates to be as "accurate" as possible ## What can go wrong? - **Errors of non-observation**: sampled elements do not make up the entire population. - Sampling - Coverage (selection-bias) - Non-response - **Errors of observation**: recorded data deviate from the truth - Interviewer - Respondents - Instrument - Method of data collection and analysis ## Sampling Error - If you do not take a census, then sampling error will be present - Probability samples control and estimate sampling error - Can be reduced with good sampling design and appropriate sample size ## Coverage Error - Sampled population does not match the target population (selection bias) ![](_images/10.1-populations.png){width=60%} - Communicate coverage errors and explain how the sampled population differs from the target population ## Coverage Error - **undercoverage**: sampling frame does not include every element of the population - **overcoverage**: sampling frame includes units **not in** the target population, or units not in the target population are not **screened out** of the sample, or double-counted ![](_images/10.1-populations.png){width=50%} ## Coverage Error - Undercoverage example:

- Overcoverage example: ## Nonresponse Error - Low response rates are not **inherently bad** - Only cause issues **if** there are systematic differences between the units that did versus did not respond - A high response rate could still miss an important part of the population - A low response rate could still be informative IF the nonrespondents looked like the respondents in all important characteristics ## Reasons for Nonresponse - Inability to contact
- Inability to respond
- Refusal

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
